title: Kenya in Brief
author: Kenya History Library
rights: Written for the Kenya History Library. Free to read and share. This short summary is no substitute for the books it points to.

chapters.title: Before the colonial state
paragraphs: People have lived in the area that is now Kenya for a very long time. The Lake Turkana basin has produced some of the most important fossils of early humans ever found, and the country is often described as a cradle of human history.

Over many centuries, farming and herding communities settled the land. Cushitic-, Nilotic- and Bantu-speaking peoples moved, traded and intermarried, building the many communities that make up Kenya today.

On the coast, towns such as Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu grew into centres of Swahili culture and Indian Ocean trade, linking East Africa with Arabia, Persia and India. The Portuguese arrived at the end of the fifteenth century and built Fort Jesus in Mombasa in the 1590s. Later, Omani rulers extended their influence along the coast.

chapters.title: Colonial rule
paragraphs: In 1895 Britain declared a protectorate over the territory, which became known as the East Africa Protectorate. The railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria, which reached Kisumu in 1901, opened the interior to settlers and to the colonial economy.

European settlers took over large areas of fertile land, especially in the central highlands, and the territory became the Colony and Protectorate of Kenya in 1920. Africans faced the loss of land, heavy taxation and pressure to work on settler farms, and had to carry a registration certificate known as the kipande.
African political organisations began to form in the 1920s, among them the Kikuyu Central Association. Demands over land, wages and representation grew through the following decades.

chapters.title: The Emergency and independence
paragraphs: In October 1952 the colonial government declared a State of Emergency in response to the Mau Mau uprising, a revolt centred on land and freedom that drew mainly on Kikuyu, Embu and Meru communities. The conflict brought mass detention, forced resettlement into villages, and violence on a large scale. Its history is still debated and remembered in Kenya today.
Jomo Kenyatta and other leaders were arrested in 1952 and convicted at Kapenguria in 1953. The Emergency was lifted in January 1960, and Kenyatta was released in 1961.

Constitutional conferences at Lancaster House in London in 1960 and 1962 prepared the way for self-government. Kenyatta became prime minister when internal self-government began in June 1963, and Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963. A year later, on 12 December 1964, it became a republic with Kenyatta as its first president.

chapters.title: Since independence
paragraphs: Kenyatta led the country until his death in August 1978. Daniel arap Moi succeeded him and governed for twenty-four years. A change to the constitution in 1982 made Kenya a one-party state in law, and a failed coup attempt followed later that year. Multiparty politics returned in 1991.

Mwai Kibaki won the 2002 election, ending Moi's rule. A disputed presidential election in December 2007 led to violence in which more than a thousand people died. The crisis ended with a power-sharing agreement mediated by an African Union panel led by Kofi Annan.

A new constitution, approved in a referendum in 2010, created 47 counties and a devolved system of government. Uhuru Kenyatta, son of the first president, served from 2013 to 2022, and William Ruto became president in 2022.

chapters.title: Where to read next
paragraphs: This summary is deliberately short. Fuller accounts include Charles Hornsby's Kenya: A History Since Independence, Daniel Branch's Kenya: Between Hope and Despair, and the final report of the Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission.
More titles will appear in this library as their rights holders give permission.
